title: Cap. X Arg. V Minor cont.: Tract. 107 — the Father’s prior giving makes them not of the world Christ does not pray for; election makes faithful, not faith elect
latin: Et Tract. 107. Per hoc quod eos illi Pater jam dedit, factum est ut non pertineant ad eum mundum pro quo non rogat Christus. Quasi dixisset, Per antecedaneam electionem factum est ut essent fideles, non per antecedaneam fidem ut essent electi.
pass_a: And Tract. 107. By this, that the Father has already given them unto him, it has been brought about that they do not belong to that world for which Christ does not pray. As if he had said, By antecedent election it has been brought about that they should be faithful, not by antecedent faith that they should be elect.
pass_b: And Tractate 107: By this—that the Father has already given them to him—it comes about that they do not belong to that world for which Christ does not pray. As if to say: antecedent election made them faithful; antecedent faith did not make them elect.

lemmas.lemma: Per hoc quod ... Pater jam dedit
lemmas.gloss: prior giving excludes them from unelected world
election precedes and produces faith

title: Cap. X Arg. V Minor: John x. 26 and 1 John ii. 19 — not believing / falling away is posterior to not being Christ’s sheep or of us; Arminius must say non-elect precedes unbeliever
latin: Jam et alteram partem Minoris pensitemus, nimirum, Quod non-credere, vel a fide incepta resilire sit posterius hac non-datione Divina, sive non-electione in Christo, et per consequens quod non-electio sive reprobatio ex tali praevisione tanquam ex antecedaneo motivo minime oriatur. De Infidelitate valde perspicuum est illud, quod antea citavimus testimonium, Joann. x. 26. Non creditis: non enim estis ex ovibus meis. Sic etiam de Apostasia a fide suscepta satis clarum est illud, 1 Joann. ii. 19. E nobis exierunt, sed ex nobis non fuerunt: nam si fuissent ex nobis, permansissent utique nobiscum, &c. Ostendat nobis Arminius, aut Corvinus quid sit non esse ex ovibus Christi, nisi non esse ex electis: quod si verum sit, tum non esse electum est quiddam prius consideratione nostra quam esse incredulum.
pass_a: Now let us also weigh the other part of the Minor, namely, That not to believe, or to spring back from faith once begun, is posterior to this Divine not-giving, or non-election in Christ, and consequently that non-election or reprobation by no means arises from such foresight as from an antecedent motive. Concerning Unbelief that testimony is very clear which we cited before, Joann. x. 26. Ye believe not: for ye are not of my sheep. So also concerning Apostasy from faith once received that is clear enough, 1 Joann. ii. 19. They went out from us, but they were not of us: for if they had been of us, they would no doubt have continued with us, &c. Let Arminius or Corvinus show us what it is not to be of Christ’s sheep, except not to be of the elect: which if it be true, then not to be elect is something prior in our consideration to being unbelieving.
pass_b: Now weigh the Minor’s other part: not believing, or springing back from faith once begun, comes after this divine not-giving—non-election in Christ—and so non-election or reprobation does not arise from such foresight as from an antecedent motive. On unbelief the witness already cited is plain (John x. 26): You do not believe, because you are not of my sheep. On apostasy from faith once received, 1 John ii. 19 is clear enough: They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would have remained with us. Let Arminius or Corvinus show what not being of Christ’s sheep means, if not not being of the elect. If that is true, then in our order of thought not being elect comes before being an unbeliever.

lemmas.gloss: unbelief posterior to not-giving

lemmas.lemma: Non creditis: non enim estis ex ovibus
lemmas.gloss: John x.26 unbelief from not being sheep
1 John ii.19 apostasy shows never of us

title: Cap. X Arg. V Minor close: apostates were never given to Christ; Augustine De corr. & grat. 7 — non-perseverance follows non-election, not foresight of non-perseverance
latin: Expediat etiam quid illud sit per quod apostatae etiam cum nobiscum sunt, non sunt tamen ex nobis. Nihil profecto aliud reperient in quo consistere possunt, praeterquam quod non fuerunt donati Christo a Patre, hoc est praeteriti, reprobati fuerunt, et in libro vitae, sive catalogo electionis Divinae, minime conscripti. Esse ergo reprobatum vel non-electum est ordine prius quam esse praevisum ut in apostasiam labentem et in eadem permanentem. Hoc recte observavit Augustinus, De corr. et grat. cap. 7. hisce verbis, Qui perseveraturi non sunt, non sunt a massa illa perditionis praescientia Dei et praedestinatione discreti, et ideo nec secundum propositum vocati, ac per hoc nec electi. Non dicit Augustinus, quia praevidebantur minime perseveraturi, ideo non fuisse electos: sed docet, eos non esse perseveraturos qui non fuerunt antecedenter electi et a massa perditionis discreti.
pass_a: Let him also unfold what that is by which apostates, even while they are with us, are nevertheless not of us. They will find nothing else in which they can rest, except that they were not given unto Christ by the Father, that is, they were passed by, reprobated, and by no means written in the book of life, or catalogue of Divine election. To be reprobate or non-elect is therefore prior in order to being foreseen as one who will fall into apostasy and remain in the same. This Augustine rightly observed, De corr. et grat. cap. 7. in these words, Those who are not going to persevere are not distinguished by the foreknowledge and predestination of God from that mass of perdition, and therefore are neither called according to purpose, and thereby neither elect. Augustine does not say, because they were foreseen as by no means going to persevere, therefore they were not elect: but he teaches that those will not persevere who were not antecedently elect and distinguished from the mass of perdition.
pass_b: Explain also that by which apostates, even while with us, are still not of us. They will find nothing to rest in except this: they were not given to Christ by the Father—passed by, reprobated, and not written in the book of life, the catalogue of divine election. So being reprobate or non-elect is prior in order to being foreseen as one who will fall into apostasy and stay there. Augustine saw this rightly (De correptione et gratia 7): Those who will not persevere are not set apart by God’s foreknowledge and predestination from that mass of perdition, and so are neither called according to purpose, nor elect. He does not say they were not elect because they were foreseen as non-persevering; he teaches that those will not persevere who were not antecedently elect and set apart from the mass of perdition.

lemmas.lemma: non fuerunt donati Christo a Patre
lemmas.gloss: apostates never given to Christ

lemmas.lemma: Qui perseveraturi non sunt ... nec electi
lemmas.gloss: non-perseverance follows non-election

title: Cap. X Arg. V close / Arg. VI open (Quinto): decree not to give faith is not productive cause of unbelief; Bradwardine — principate over futures and non-futures
latin: Sed ne quis inde errandi occasionem arripiat quod dictum est, non-dare Christo vel non-eligere esse prius considerandum ex parte Dei reprobantis, quam non-credere aut non-perseverare absolute praevideatur ex parte personae reprobatae; id moneo non esse ita intelligendum, quasi Deus, aut Dei decretum, causa productiva esset infidelitatis, apostasiae, aut pertinaciae humanae, (haec enim omnia nascuntur ex insita hominum corruptione) sed quia cum fides et perseverantia sint dona Dei miserentis, quae omnibus posset impertire, ipso actu reprobandi decernat apud se non efficere in aliquibus, quod in aliis effecturus est, quodque in omnibus efficere potuisset. Nam (ut vere Augustinus, De corr. et grat. cap. 24.) Deo volenti salvum facere nullum hominum resistit arbitrium. Ipsum itaque resistere, sive in infidelitate perseverare, quod praevidetur in omnibus reprobates, aperte evincit illum qui habet humanorum cordium quocunque placuerit inclinandorum omnipotentissimam potestatem, ut inquit Augustinus ibidem, non habuisse hanc efficacem hosce salvandi voluntatem: quod nil aliud est quam eos non-elegisse sive reprobasse. Quinto arguitur ab illo principatu qui Deo tribuendus est, non modo circa res futuras, sed etiam circa res non futuras. Nam (ut recte statuit Bradwardinus, lib. 3. c. 33.) Deus non solum super entia, sed etiam super non-entia tenet principatum.
pass_a: But lest anyone snatch from what has been said an occasion of erring, namely that not-giving unto Christ or not-electing is to be considered prior on God’s part who reprobates, before not-believing or not-persevering is absolutely foreseen on the part of the reprobate person; I warn that this is not so to be understood as if God, or God’s decree, were the productive cause of human unbelief, apostasy, or pertinacity (for all these are born from the inbred corruption of men), but because, since faith and perseverance are gifts of God who shows mercy, which he could impart to all, by the very act of reprobating he decrees with himself not to effect in some what he is going to effect in others, and what he could have effected in all. For (as Augustine truly says, De corr. et grat. cap. 24.) No human will resists God willing to make safe. That very resisting, therefore, or persevering in unbelief, which is foreseen in all the reprobate, openly proves that he who has the most omnipotent power of inclining human hearts whithersoever it has pleased him, as Augustine says in the same place, did not have this efficacious will of saving these: which is nothing other than not to have elected them, or to have reprobated them. Fifthly it is argued from that principate which is to be ascribed unto God, not only concerning future things, but also concerning things not future. For (as Bradwardine rightly establishes, lib. 3. c. 33.) God holds principate not only over beings, but also over non-beings.
pass_b: But lest anyone twist what was said—that not giving to Christ, or not electing, is prior on God’s reprobating side to absolute foresight of not-believing or not-persevering on the reprobate’s side—I warn: this does not mean God or his decree is the productive cause of human unbelief, apostasy, or stubbornness (those spring from inbred corruption). It means that since faith and perseverance are gifts of the merciful God, which he could give to all, by the very act of reprobating he decrees not to work in some what he will work in others and could have worked in all. For as Augustine truly says (De correptione et gratia 24), no human will resists God when he wills to save. So that very resisting—or persevering in unbelief—foreseen in all the reprobate plainly proves that he who holds most omnipotent power to incline human hearts wherever he pleases did not have this efficacious will to save these; which is nothing other than not electing them, or reprobating them. Fifth, the argument is from that principate due to God not only over future things but also over non-future things. For as Bradwardine rightly holds (lib. 3, c. 33), God holds principate not only over beings but also over non-beings.

lemmas.gloss: decree not productive cause of unbelief
Arg. VI: principate over futures and non-futures
Bradwardine: principate over non-beings

title: Cap. X Arg. VI: principate forces the issue — non-futurity of faith in some cannot rest on bare foresight; will decrees efficacious operation or its denial
latin: Hoc posito, cum ab aeterno certum Deo sit et definitum, quod in quibusdam hominibus nec poenitentia, nec fides, nec perseverantia unquam sit futura, quaeso quorsum reducemus harum rerum non futurarum principatum ad Divinam voluntatem? Non possumus affirmare aeternam Dei voluntatem, aut decretum aliquod Divinum, in istis hominibus efficere sive gignere infidelitatem, impoenitentiam et apostasiam: Deus enim autor non est ejus rei cujus est ultor. Neque sufficit dicere, Deum ab aeterno praevidisse, quod tales homines, administrata illis gratia sufficienti ad poenitendum, credendum et perseverandum, propria sua malitia exsisterent impoenitentes, infideles aut apostatae. Nam hoc Deo quidem tribuit rerum futurarum aut non futurarum praescientiam infallibilem, sed interim humanae voluntati adscribit de futura earundem existentia aut non-futura determinationem principalem.
pass_a: This being laid down, since it is certain and defined unto God from eternity that in certain men neither repentance, nor faith, nor perseverance will ever be future, I ask: whither shall we reduce the principate of these non-future things unto the Divine will? We cannot affirm that the eternal will of God, or some Divine decree, effects or begets in those men unbelief, impenitence, and apostasy: for God is not the author of that thing of which he is the avenger. Nor does it suffice to say that God from eternity foresaw that such men, sufficient grace having been administered unto them for repenting, believing, and persevering, would by their own malice exist as impenitent, unbelieving, or apostates. For this indeed ascribes unto God infallible foreknowledge of things future or not future, but meantime ascribes unto the human will the principal determination concerning their future existence or non-futurity.
pass_b: That granted: since it is certain and defined for God from eternity that in some men neither repentance nor faith nor perseverance will ever come to be, where do we lodge the principate over these non-futures in the divine will? We cannot say God’s eternal will or some divine decree effects or begets unbelief, impenitence, and apostasy in those men—for God is not author of what he avenges. Nor is it enough to say he foresaw from eternity that such men, given sufficient grace to repent, believe, and persevere, would by their own malice prove impenitent, unbelieving, or apostate. That gives God infallible foresight of futures and non-futures, but still leaves the human will the principal determination of whether those things will exist or not.

lemmas.gloss: where to lodge principate of non-futures
God not author of what he avenges
bare foresight leaves determination to man

title: Cap. X Arg. VI: therefore God’s will predominates — Cain/Judas/Hymenaeus vs Peter/Paul; reprobation’s non-gift of faith precedes foreseen unbelief
latin: Eo igitur tandem redeundum est, ut fateamur penes Deum esse principalem rerum futurarum et non-futurarum determinationem; quatenus in bonis actibus decrevit ad eos producendos efficacem suam operationem adhibere; quatenus in malis, quae ab hominibus improbis producuntur, decrevit eos minime impedire; denique, quatenus in bonis actibus, qui ab iisdem omitterentur, decrevit non dare gratiam efficacem qua fierent. Et sic voluntas Dei est causa predominans et praedeterminans quoad non-esse rerum minime futurarum, quoniam cum possit facere ut essent futurae si vellet, non vult tamen hoc facere quod posset. Jam vero ab aeterno non velle facere cum posset, ut Cain poeniteat, ut Judas credat, ut Hymenaeus perseveret, est antecedaneae non-electionis firma demonstratio; sicut velle efficere ut Petrus poeniteat, ut Paulus credat et perseveret, est antecedaneae electionis clara probatio. Hoc autem reprobationis decretum, quod continet determinatum actum Divinae voluntatis de non danda fide, poenitentia, perseverantia certis quibusdam personis, earundem infidelitatem, impoenitentiam et praevisam et certo futuram praecedat est necesse.
pass_a: We must therefore at length return hither, that we confess that with God is the principal determination of things future and not-future; inasmuch as in good acts he has decreed to apply his efficacious operation unto producing them; inasmuch as in evils which are produced by wicked men, he has decreed by no means to hinder them; finally, inasmuch as in good acts which would be omitted by the same, he has decreed not to give the efficacious grace by which they would be done. And thus the will of God is the predominating and predetermining cause as to the non-being of things by no means future, because although he can make them future if he wills, yet he does not will to do this which he could. Now truly not to will from eternity to do, when he could, that Cain should repent, that Judas should believe, that Hymenaeus should persevere, is a firm demonstration of antecedent non-election; just as to will to effect that Peter should repent, that Paul should believe and persevere, is a clear proof of antecedent election. But this decree of reprobation, which contains the determined act of the Divine will concerning faith, repentance, perseverance not to be given unto certain persons, must of necessity precede their unbelief, impenitence, both foreseen and certainly future.
pass_b: So we must come back to this: with God lies the principal determination of futures and non-futures—in good acts, by decreeing to apply his efficacious operation to produce them; in evils produced by the wicked, by decreeing not to hinder them; and in good acts those same would omit, by decreeing not to give the efficacious grace by which they would be done. Thus God’s will is the predominating, predetermining cause of the non-being of things that will not be: he can make them future if he wills, yet he does not will to do what he could. Not willing from eternity—though he could—that Cain repent, Judas believe, Hymenaeus persevere, firmly demonstrates antecedent non-election; willing to bring about that Peter repent, Paul believe and persevere, clearly proves antecedent election. And this reprobation decree—the determined act of the divine will not to give faith, repentance, perseverance to certain persons—must precede their unbelief and impenitence, foreseen and certainly future.

lemmas.gloss: principal determination with God
non-will to save shows non-election
non-gift of faith precedes foreseen unbelief

title: Cap. X Arg. VI close: unbelief foreseen in negation of efficacious grace; Augustine De praedest. sanct. 6 — preparing / not preparing the will precedes foresight of faith or unbelief
latin: Non ergo reprobatio ponenda est ex praevisione antecedaneae infidelitatis, nec electio ex praevisione fidei; sed infidelitas reprobatorum finalis praevidetur in antecedente negatione gratiae efficacis, et fides electorum perseverans praevidetur in antecedente praeparatione gratiae efficacis: ut utrobique principatus, authoritas, superioritas et determinativa potestas sive rerum futurarum sive non-futurarum sit penes Deum tanquam supremum arbitrum. Hoc illud est quod docuit Augustinus, de praedest. sanct. cap. 6. Alii credunt, alii contradictunt. Volunt ergo isti credere; nolunt autem illi. Quis hoc ignoret? quis hoc neget? Sed cum aliis praeparetur, aliis non praeparetur voluntas a Domino, &c. Unde patet decretum de praeparandis et non praeparandis humanis voluntatibus esse praevisa sive fide sive infidelitate humana prius: Quod perinde est ac si diceremus, praedestinationem et praeteritionem singularium personarum esse absoluta praescientia fidei aut infidelitatis in eisdem priorem.
pass_a: Therefore reprobation is not to be placed from foresight of antecedent unbelief, nor election from foresight of faith; but the final unbelief of the reprobate is foreseen in the antecedent negation of efficacious grace, and the persevering faith of the elect is foreseen in the antecedent preparation of efficacious grace: so that on both sides principate, authority, superiority, and determinative power, whether of things future or not-future, may be with God as supreme arbiter. This is that which Augustine taught, de praedest. sanct. cap. 6. Some believe, others contradict. These therefore will to believe; but those will not. Who is ignorant of this? who denies this? But since unto some the will is prepared by the Lord, unto others it is not prepared, &c. Whence it is plain that the decree concerning human wills to be prepared and not to be prepared is prior to foresight either of human faith or of unbelief: Which is just as if we should say that the predestination and preterition of singular persons is prior to absolute foreknowledge of faith or unbelief in the same.
pass_b: So reprobation is not to be set from foresight of antecedent unbelief, nor election from foresight of faith. Final unbelief in the reprobate is foreseen in the antecedent denial of efficacious grace; persevering faith in the elect is foreseen in the antecedent preparation of that grace—so that on both sides principate, authority, superiority, and determining power over futures and non-futures rest with God as supreme arbiter. That is what Augustine taught (De praedestinatione sanctorum 6): Some believe; others contradict. These will to believe; those will not. Who does not know this? Who denies it? But since the Lord prepares the will for some and not for others, and so on. So the decree to prepare or not prepare human wills is prior to foresight of human faith or unbelief—which is as much as to say that predestination and preterition of singular persons is prior to absolute foreknowledge of faith or unbelief in them.

lemmas.gloss: unbelief foreseen in denied efficacious grace
Augustine: preparing the will precedes foresight

title: Cap. X Arg. VII open: Arminius’s three decrees leave church-acquisition to free will; Grevinchovius and Episcopius admit redemption may apply to none / church may wholly fail
latin: Si, ut ponit Arminius, post decretum Dei de dando Christo Mediatore et Salvatore, et illud alterum quo decrevit quosvis sub conditione resipiscentiae, fidei et perseverantiae salvos facere, itemque et illud tertium quo decrevit media ad resipiscentiam et fidem necessaria omnibus administrare; si, inquam, positis hisce tribus decretis, singularium personarum electio et reprobatio, salus et damnatio dependeat ex praevisa hominum sive fide sive infidelitate, tum sequitur, hominum libero arbitrio relictum fuisse, ut possent finem Dominicae passionis, hoc est, acquisitionem Ecclesiae, prorsus evacuare: Ita ut, quod Christus frustra mortuus non fuerit, quod habeat Ecclesiam electorum sanguine suo efficaciter redemptam, non ex antecedaneo aliquo decreto, aut speciali gratia Dei membra quaedam Christo Capiti eligentis et per Christum vivificanda et salvanda praedestinantis, sed ex contingente operatione humanarum voluntatum evenerit. Universi enim mortales, si considerentur ut nondum electi, nec speciali illa providentia Dei, quam Praedestinationem vocamus, ad habendam fidem et perseverandum in eadem praedeterminati, possunt in sua incredulitate manere, possunt a fide suscepta resilire, possunt, uno verbo, a salute excidere, et Christum Redemptorem, absque Ecclesia redempta prorsus relinquere. Hanc consequentiam non possunt negare, qui electionem et reprobationem ex praevisione fidei et infidelitatis conantur arcessere. Ingenue itaque illam admisit Grevinchovius, Dissert. De morte Christi, pag. 14. Asserimus, inquit, potuisse omnibus impetratam esse redemptionem, et tamen nullis applicatam propter intervenientem omnium infidelitatem. Sic etiam Episcopius hoc principio Arminiano innixus, fatetur totam Ecclesiam in terris deficere posse, neque necesse esse ad hoc, ut Christus Rex et Caput maneat, illum habere semper Ecclesiam aliquam veram in terris.
pass_a: If, as Arminius lays down, after God’s decree of giving Christ as Mediator and Saviour, and that other by which he decreed to make safe whomsoever under the condition of repentance, faith, and perseverance, and likewise also that third by which he decreed to administer unto all the means necessary unto repentance and faith; if, I say, these three decrees being laid down, the election and reprobation of singular persons, salvation and damnation, depend from foresight of men’s faith or unbelief, then it follows that it was left unto men’s free will that they could utterly evacuate the end of the Lord’s passion, that is, the acquisition of the Church: So that, that Christ was not dead in vain, that he has a Church of elect efficaciously redeemed by his blood, would have come about not from some antecedent decree, or special grace of God electing certain members unto Christ the Head and predestining them to be quickened and saved through Christ, but from the contingent operation of human wills. For all mortals, if they be considered as not yet elect, nor predetermined by that special providence of God which we call Predestination unto having faith and persevering in the same, can remain in their unbelief, can spring back from faith once received, can, in a word, fall from salvation, and leave Christ the Redeemer altogether without a redeemed Church. They cannot deny this consequence who try to fetch election and reprobation from foresight of faith and unbelief. Grevinchovius therefore candidly admitted it, Dissert. De morte Christi, pag. 14. We assert, he says, that redemption could have been obtained for all, and yet applied to none because of the intervening unbelief of all. So also Episcopius, resting on this Arminian principle, confesses that the whole Church on earth can fail, and that it is not necessary, for Christ to remain King and Head, that he always have some true Church on earth.
pass_b: If, as Arminius sets it, after God’s decree to give Christ as Mediator and Savior, and the second decree to save any under the condition of repentance, faith, and perseverance, and the third to administer to all the means needed for repentance and faith—if, with those three decrees in place, election and reprobation of singular persons, salvation and damnation, hang on foresight of men’s faith or unbelief—then it follows that free will was left able to empty out the end of the Lord’s passion, the acquiring of the Church. So that Christ not dying in vain, and having a church of elect efficaciously redeemed by his blood, would come not from some antecedent decree or special grace of God electing certain members to Christ the Head and predestining them to be made alive and saved through him, but from the contingent working of human wills. For all mortals, if taken as not yet elect and not predetermined by that special providence we call Predestination to have faith and persevere in it, can stay in unbelief, spring back from faith once received, in a word fall from salvation and leave Christ the Redeemer with no redeemed church at all. Those who fetch election and reprobation from foresight of faith and unbelief cannot deny this consequence. Grevinchovius admitted it candidly (Dissert. De morte Christi, p. 14): We assert that redemption could have been obtained for all, and yet applied to none because of the intervening unbelief of all. So Episcopius, resting on this Arminian principle, confesses the whole church on earth can fail, and that Christ need not always have some true church on earth in order to remain King and Head.

lemmas.gloss: three decrees leave church-acquisition to free will
redemption obtained for all, applied to none
whole earthly church may fail
